title: SOLID & code design
subtitle: Practice making code easier to change.
description: Learn SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, and DIP through code that needs to change or is difficult to test. Recognize code smells and decide when an interface or a separate class helps.

lessons.title: Single Responsibility Principle
lessons.summary: Separate responsibilities that change for different reasons, such as pricing, storage, and notifications.
objectives: Identify classes with unrelated reasons to change.
keyPoints: SRP concerns reasons to change, not the number of methods.
A class serving unrelated business actors may need to be split.
Keep calculations separate from database and email operations.
practice: Split an OrderManager that calculates totals, saves orders, and emails receipts into separate classes.
Changing an email template does not change pricing code.

exercises.prompt: According to SRP, what does “one responsibility” mean?
options: One reason to change, usually associated with one actor requesting changes.
exercises.explanation: SRP groups behavior that changes for the same reason. Method counts and line limits do not identify that boundary.

exercises.prompt: Which methods do not belong in PriceCalculator?
exercises.explanation: Persistence and email delivery change for different reasons than pricing. Put them in a repository and notifier.

lessons.title: Open/Closed Principle
lessons.summary: Add a new variation through an implementation rather than editing stable business flow.
objectives: Add a new discount strategy through an interface.
keyPoints: An interface can provide an extension point for a known variation.
Checkout can call DiscountPolicy without knowing each discount type.
Introduce abstractions when the need is concrete.
practice: The new discount works through the existing DiscountPolicy contract.

exercises.prompt: Add PromoDiscount without changing Checkout. Implement DiscountPolicy and return the subtotal after a 20% discount.
exercises.explanation: Checkout calls policy.apply(subtotal). The new policy supplies behavior without changing that flow.

exercises.prompt: A team has one shipping method and no plans for another. What is the most sensible next step?
options: Keep a simple implementation and extract an interface when another real variation appears.
Build an interface, factory, and plugin loader immediately.
Copy the implementation whenever a variation is needed.
exercises.explanation: Abstractions add maintenance work. Introduce a variation point once its requirements are clear.

lessons.title: Liskov Substitution & Interface Segregation
lessons.summary: Implementations must fulfill their contracts. Split interfaces so clients only depend on operations they use.
objectives: Recognize implementations that break a parent contract.
Split read and write interfaces according to client needs.
keyPoints: A subtype should not strengthen preconditions or weaken promised results.
Throwing UnsupportedOperationException can reveal a contract mismatch.
Small client-specific interfaces make test fakes simpler.
practice: Split OrderRepository into OrderReader and OrderWriter.
A reporting component can use OrderReader without implementing save.

exercises.prompt: ReadOnlyOrderRepository implements OrderRepository but throws UnsupportedOperationException from save(). Which principle is most directly violated?
options: Liskov Substitution: callers do not receive the behavior promised by OrderRepository.
None; this is always a standard pattern.
exercises.explanation: The implementation cannot fulfill the write contract. Splitting read and write interfaces lets it implement only the supported behavior.

exercises.prompt: Split the interface into OrderReader with findById and OrderWriter with save.
exercises.explanation: Read-only clients depend on OrderReader. A JPA repository can implement both contracts.

lessons.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
lessons.summary: Business logic uses an interface that fits its needs. Technical implementations follow that interface.
objectives: Depend on an interface rather than a concrete gateway.
keyPoints: High-level and low-level modules both depend on abstractions.
The business-facing interface should describe what the business needs.
Dependency injection is a technique; dependency inversion is a design principle.
practice: Refactor Checkout to receive PaymentGateway instead of constructing BankGateway.
A test can pass FakeGateway without starting Spring or contacting a bank.

exercises.prompt: Refactor Checkout to accept PaymentGateway in its constructor and store it in a private final field. Do not create BankGateway inside Checkout.
checks: Assign the constructor argument to the field
Do not call new BankGateway() inside Checkout
exercises.explanation: The caller, test, or Spring container now chooses the implementation. Checkout only knows the interface.

exercises.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes DI and DIP?
options: DI supplies dependencies from outside; DIP concerns the direction of dependencies toward abstractions.
They mean exactly the same thing.
exercises.explanation: Injecting a concrete BankGateway is DI, but the business code still depends on a technical implementation. Depending on PaymentGateway also applies DIP.

exercises.prompt: Put these steps in a safe order when applying DIP to Checkout.
items: Write characterization tests for the current Checkout behavior.
Extract PaymentGateway from the methods Checkout uses.
Change Checkout to receive PaymentGateway through its constructor.
Switch tests to FakeGateway and run the full suite again.
exercises.explanation: Establish the existing behavior first, then extract the interface and change construction while keeping tests passing.
